regulation_content.regulation_text:
1. Short title and commencement

 (1) These regulations may be called the International Financial Services
 Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024.

 (2) They shall come into force on the date of publication in the Official Gazette.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 1, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.1
regulation_content.simple_explanation: This is the name-and-start-date clause. It gives the rules their official name — the IFSCA (Listing) Regulations, 2024 — and says they take effect on the day they are published in the Official Gazette (the government's official record), not the day they are signed. So whenever you need to know 'from what date do these rules apply?', use the Gazette publication date.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The commencement peg is publication, not the notification date printed on the cover, so build your regulatory timeline from the Gazette date. The instrument supersedes the 2021 Issuance and Listing framework (see Reg 131), which matters when reading older offer documents and precedents.
regulation_content.practical_point: Record the Gazette publication date in the source register and treat 29-Aug-2024 as the commencement anchor for grandfathering questions.
regulation_content.applicability: All entities seeking to list securities or permitted financial products on a recognised stock exchange in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.regulation_text:
2. Objective

 These regulations provide the regulatory framework for listing of specified
 securities, debt securities, depository receipts and other permitted financial
 products on the recognised stock exchanges in the International Financial
 Services Centres in India.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 2, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.1
regulation_content.simple_explanation: This clause simply states why the rules exist: to set out how shares, bonds, depository receipts and other approved products can be listed on the stock exchanges in IFSC (the GIFT City international financial centre). It does not create any duty by itself. It is mainly useful as a guide when another rule is unclear and you need to understand the intention behind it.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: An objective clause is a reading aid, not an operative obligation. It is useful for purposive interpretation where a later provision is ambiguous, but it creates no duty on its own.
regulation_content.applicability: All entities seeking to list securities or permitted financial products on a recognised stock exchange in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.regulation_text:
3. Definitions

 (1) In these regulations, unless the context otherwise requires, the terms
 defined herein shall bear the meanings assigned to them below, and their
 cognate expressions and variations shall be construed accordingly, -

 (a) “Act” means the International Financial Services Centres Authority
 Act, 2019 (50 of 2019);

 (b)“Banking Unit” means a unit licensed or permitted by the Authority to
 undertake permissible activities under International Financial Services
 Centres Authority (Banking) Regulations, 2020;

 (c) “business combination” means a merger or amalgamation or
 acquisition of shares or assets of one or more companies having
 business operations by a Special Purpose Acquisition Company;

 (d) “certificate of deposit” means a negotiable, unsecured money market
 instrument issued in dematerialised form or as a Usance Promissory
 Note against funds deposited at a Banking Unit for a maturity period
 upto one year;

(e) “commercial paper” means an unsecured money market instrument
 issued in the form of promissory note;

(f) “control” shall include the right to appoint majority of the directors or
 to control the management or policy decisions exercisable by a person
 or persons acting individually or in concert, directly or indirectly,
 including by virtue of their shareholding or management rights or
 shareholders agreements or voting agreements or in any other manner;

(g) “controlling shareholder” shall include a person who has control over
 the affairs of the issuer, directly or indirectly whether as a shareholder,
 director or otherwise;

(h) “convertible debt instrument” means an instrument which creates or
 acknowledges indebtedness and is convertible into equity shares of the
 issuer at a later date with or without the option of the holder of the
 instrument, whether constituting a charge on the assets of the issuer or
 not;

(i) “convertible preference shares” means preference shares which can be
 converted into a predetermined number of ordinary shares usually after
 a specified date or upon the occurrence of certain events;

(j) “convertible securities” means securities which are convertible into or
 exchangeable with equity shares of the issuer at a later date, with or
 without the option of the holder of such securities and includes
 convertible debt instruments and convertible preference shares;

(k) “debt securities” means non-convertible debt securities which create or
 acknowledge indebtedness and includes debentures, notes and bonds;

(l) “depository receipt (DR)” means a negotiable financial instrument
 representing underlying securities of an issuer in another jurisdiction;

(m) “designated stock exchange” means a recognised stock exchange
 chosen by the issuer on which the securities or any other permitted
 financial product is listed or proposed to be listed for the purpose of a
 particular issue of securities or a financial product under these
 regulations;

(n) "Foreign Jurisdiction" means a country, other than India, whose
 securities market regulator is a signatory to International Organization
 of Securities Commission’s Multilateral Memorandum of
 Understanding or a signatory to a bilateral Memorandum of
 Understanding with the Authority, and which is not identified in the
 public statement of Financial Action Task Force as:

 (i) a jurisdiction having a strategic Anti-Money Laundering
 or Combating the Financing of Terrorism deficiencies to
 which counter measures apply; or

 (ii) a jurisdiction that has not made sufficient progress in
 addressing the deficiencies or has not committed to an
 action plan developed with the Financial Action Task
 Force to address the deficiencies;

(o) “follow-on public offer (FPO)” or “further public offer” means an offer
 of specified securities by a Listed Entity to the public for subscription
 and includes an offer for sale of specified securities to the public by
 any existing holder of such specified securities in a listed issuer;

(p) “green shoe option” means an option of allotting specified securities in
 excess of the specified shares offered in the public issue as a post-
 listing price stabilizing mechanism;

(q) "group entity" means an entity of a business group that consists of a
 parent company or of any other type of legal person exercising control
 over the rest of the group, together with branches and/or subsidiaries;

(r) “IFSCA” or “Authority” means the International Financial Services
 Centres Authority established under sub-section (1) of section 4 of the
 Act;

(s) “information memorandum" means a document that provides investors
 with information about the issuer and the securities in connection with
 an application for listing of securities and includes an offering
 memorandum or an offering circular;

(t) “initial public offer (IPO)” means an offer of specified securities by an
 unlisted issuer to the public for subscription and includes an offer for
 sale of specified securities to the public by any existing holder of such
 specified securities in an unlisted issuer;

(u) “issuer” means an entity which makes or proposes to make or has made
 an issue of specified securities or debt securities or depository receipts
 or commercial paper or certificates of deposit or any other permitted
 financial products and intends to list on a recognised stock exchange
 under these regulations;

(v) "International Financial Services Centre (IFSC)” shall have the same
 meaning as assigned to it under clause (g) of sub-section (1) of Section
 3 of the Act;

(w) “key managerial personnel”, in relation to a company incorporated in
 India, shall have the same meaning as assigned to it under clause (51)
 of section 2 of the Companies Act, 2013, and in relation to a company
 incorporated outside India shall mean:

 (i) the chief executive officer or the managing director or the
 manager;

 (ii) the company secretary or the corporate secretary;

 (iii) a whole-time director;

 (iv) the chief financial officer; and

 (v) such other officer as may be designated as key managerial
 personnel by the Board of the company;

(x) “lead manager” means an investment banker registered with the
 Authority and appointed by the issuer to manage the issue and in case
 of a book built issue, the lead manager(s) appointed by the issuer shall

 act as the book running lead manager(s) for the purposes of book
 building;

 (y) “Listed Entity” means an entity whose specified securities or debt
 securities or depository receipts or any other permitted financial
 products are listed on a recognised stock exchange under these
 regulations;

 (z) “offer document” includes a red herring prospectus, prospectus, shelf
 prospectus, letter of offer, tranche prospectus, placement
 memorandum, as applicable;

 (aa) “promoter” shall have the same meaning as assigned to it under clause
 (69) of section 2 of the Companies Act, 2013:

 Explanation: The references to “promoter” under these regulations
 shall apply only in respect of companies incorporated under the
 Companies Act, 2013;

 (bb) “qualified institutions placement” means issue of specified
 securities to qualified institutional buyers on a private placement basis and
 includes an offer for sale of specified securities by the promoters or
 controlling shareholders on a private placement basis;

 (cc) “recognised stock exchange” means a stock exchange recognised by
 the Authority;

 (dd) “securities”, for the purposes of these regulations, shall mean
 specified securities, debt securities and depository receipts listed or
 proposed to be listed on a recognised stock exchange;

 (ee) “Special Purpose Acquisition Company (SPAC)” means a company
 which does not have any operating business and has been formed with
 the primary objective to effect a business combination;

 (ff) “specified securities” means equity shares and convertible securities;

 (gg) “Superior Right equity shares” or “SR equity shares” means such class
 of equity shares of an issuer which grants their holders voting rights
 superior to the ordinary equity shares issued by that issuer;

 (hh) “underwriter” means a person who engages in the business of
 underwriting of an issue of securities of a body corporate.

 (2) Words and expressions used and not defined in these regulations but
 defined in the Act, the Companies Act, 2013, the Securities Contracts
 (Regulation) Act, 1956, the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act,
 1992, the Depositories Act, 1996, or any rules or regulations made
 thereunder shall have the same meanings as respectively assigned to them
 in those Acts, rules or regulations made thereunder or any statutory
 modification or re-enactment thereto, as the case may be.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 3, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.1
regulation_content.simple_explanation: This is the dictionary of the rules. It gives the meaning of the important terms used throughout. Anything not defined here takes its meaning from the main laws — the IFSCA Act, Companies Act, securities laws and so on. Two definitions matter a lot in practice: 'Foreign Jurisdiction' (a country counts only if its regulator has the right international tie-ups and a clean anti-money-laundering standing), and 'promoter' (this idea applies only to companies set up under the Indian Companies Act, so it may not apply to a foreign company at all).
regulation_content.regmate_comment: Two definitions repay close reading. 'Foreign Jurisdiction' is gated on IOSCO MMoU / bilateral MoU status and FATF standing, so an issuer's home-country regulator status can decide eligibility before any financial test. The 'promoter' concept applies only to companies incorporated under the Companies Act 2013 (see the Explanation), which changes how you read lock-up and eligibility for foreign issuers.
regulation_content.practical_point: When onboarding an issuer, first classify its home jurisdiction against the 'Foreign Jurisdiction' test and confirm whether the 'promoter' concept applies at all.
regulation_content.interview_point: Why does the 'promoter' definition matter differently for a Cayman-incorporated issuer versus an Indian company listing in GIFT IFSC?

regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 4, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.4
regulation_content.simple_explanation: This tells you which transactions the rules cover. It is decided by the type of deal, not the type of company. Covered deals include: a first sale of shares to the public (IPO) and a later sale by an already-listed company (FPO); SPAC IPOs; rights, preferential and QIP issues; issuing and listing depository receipts and bonds; secondary listings; and listing commercial paper, certificates of deposit and other approved products. The same company can fall under different chapters for different products.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: Applicability is transaction-led, not entity-led. The same issuer can fall under different chapters for different products, so map the specific route before picking the obligations that follow.

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.regulation_text:
5. General Principles

 The underlying principles for an issuer proposing to list its securities or any
 other permitted financial product on the recognised stock exchange(s) are as
 under:

 (a) There should be true, correct and adequate disclosure of material
 information in the offer document to enable the investors to take an
 informed decision.

 (b) There should be full, accurate and timely disclosure of financial results,
 risk and other non-financial information which may be material for
 investors to take an informed decision;

 (c) All holders shall be treated in a fair and equitable manner;

 (d) The directors of an issuer shall ensure to act in the best interest of all
 stakeholders.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 5, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.5
regulation_content.simple_explanation: These are the ground rules of fair disclosure that run through everything. In short: tell investors the full and correct material facts; share financial and other important information on time; treat all investors fairly; and let directors act in the interest of everyone with a stake. When a specific rule is silent, the regulator falls back on these principles to judge whether a company behaved properly.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: These principles are the interpretive backbone the Authority will fall back on where a specific rule is silent. In practice they are read into the due-diligence and materiality judgments made under Regs 16 and 87.
regulation_content.applicability: All issuers proposing to list on a recognised stock exchange in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.regulation_text:
6. General Eligibility Criteria

 (1) An issuer shall be eligible to list its securities or any other permitted
 financial product on a recognised stock exchange subject to the following
 conditions:

 (a) the issuer is incorporated or set up either in an IFSC or in India or
 in a Foreign Jurisdiction, in accordance with the relevant laws of
 its home jurisdiction;

 (b) the issuer operates in conformity with its constitution; and

 (c) the issuer is eligible to issue such securities or other financial
 products, that are proposed to be listed on the recognised stock
 exchange, in conformity with the relevant laws of its home
 jurisdiction.

 Provided that a public Indian company proposing to list its equity shares
 on a recognised stock exchange shall also be required to meet the eligibility

 criteria provided under Schedule XI of the Foreign Exchange Management
 (Non-debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 and the Companies (Listing of equity
 shares in permissible jurisdictions) Rules, 2024.

 Explanation: The following entities shall also be eligible to list its debt
 securities on a recognised stock exchange:

 (a) a supranational or a multilateral or a statutory institution;

 (b) a municipality or any similar body; and

 (c) an entity which offers or proposes to offer sovereign debt
 securities.

 (2) An issuer shall not be eligible to list its securities if the issuer or any of its
 promoters or controlling shareholders or directors or the existing
 shareholders offering shares in the issue is -

 (a) debarred from accessing the capital market; or

 (b) a wilful defaulter; or

 (c) a fugitive economic offender.
 Explanation: For the purpose of these regulations, ‘wilful defaulter’ or
 ‘fugitive economic offender’, by whatever name called, means a person
 who is categorized as such, as per relevant laws of its home jurisdiction.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 6, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.5
regulation_content.simple_explanation: This sets the basic 'who is allowed to list' test. The company must be properly incorporated (in IFSC, India or an approved foreign country), follow its own charter, and be allowed to issue the securities it plans to. It is blocked if the company or its key people (promoters, controlling shareholders, directors) are banned from the markets, are wilful defaulters (deliberately did not repay loans), or are declared fugitive economic offenders. One extra point: an Indian public company listing shares must also clear India's FEMA foreign-investment conditions and the MCA's overseas-listing rules — clearing IFSCA alone is not enough.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The proviso quietly imports Indian law for one class of issuer: a public Indian company listing equity must also clear Schedule XI of the FEM (NDI) Rules 2019 and the Companies (Listing of equity shares in permissible jurisdictions) Rules 2024. That cross-statutory overlay is the point candidates most often miss — IFSCA eligibility is necessary but not sufficient for an Indian issuer.
regulation_content.practical_point: Run a background check early on the company and its promoters, controlling shareholders and directors (any bans, defaults or offender status). For an Indian company, also add the FEMA and MCA overseas-listing checks to your list, because these are easy to overlook and can stop the deal.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Maintain documentary evidence of incorporation, constitutional conformity, and clean status (no debarment / wilful default / FEO) for the issuer and named persons, refreshed at filing.
regulation_content.example: Say an Indian company, Aster Ltd, wants to list its shares on an IFSC exchange. Even if it ticks every IFSCA box, it still cannot list until it also satisfies India's FEMA rules and the company-law rules for listing abroad. IFSCA approval is necessary, but not the full story for an Indian company.
regulation_content.risk_point: Inspectors look closely at the background check on the key people, and — for Indian companies — at whether the FEMA/MCA conditions were actually met and evidenced, not just assumed.
regulation_content.applicability: All issuers proposing to list on a recognised stock exchange in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.regulation_text:
7. Dematerialised Form

 The securities and other permitted financial products listed or proposed to be
 listed on a recognised stock exchange shall be freely transferable and held in
 dematerialised form:

 Provided that debt securities and such other financial products may also be held
 with an international central securities depository.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 7, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.6
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Listed securities must be freely transferable (a buyer can freely take ownership) and held in electronic (demat) form rather than paper. Bonds and some products can also be held through an international depository. The catch: if the company's charter or a shareholder agreement restricts transfers, that restriction has to be removed before listing — you cannot just disclose it and carry on.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: Free transferability and demat are pre-conditions, not post-listing housekeeping. Any transfer restriction embedded in the constitution or a shareholders' agreement must be resolved before listing, not disclosed around.
regulation_content.applicability: All issuers proposing to list on a recognised stock exchange in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.regulation_text:
8. Currency

 The securities and other permitted financial products shall be denominated in a
 specified foreign currency for listing and trading on a recognised stock
 exchange:

 Explanation 1: for the purpose of these regulations, specified foreign currency
 shall mean the currency specified in the First Schedule of the International
 Financial Services Centres Authority (Banking) Regulations, 2020 or any other
 regulation notified by the Authority.

 Explanation 2: For the purpose of these regulations, reference to USD shall
 mean an equivalent amount in the currency in which such securities are issued.

 CHAPTER III: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND
 FPO)

PART A: INITIAL PUBLIC OFFER
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 8, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.6
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Everything listed and traded here must be priced in an approved foreign currency (like USD), not Indian rupees. Because the rules quote thresholds in US dollars, any dollar figure just means 'that amount in whatever approved currency the issue uses'. So if an issue is in euros, read every USD limit as the euro equivalent.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The 'specified foreign currency' is drawn from the IFSCA (Banking) Regulations, 2020 First Schedule. Every USD threshold in these regulations is therefore a currency-equivalent test, which matters when pricing an issue denominated in EUR or GBP.
regulation_content.applicability: All issuers proposing to list on a recognised stock exchange in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
9. Eligibility criteria

 An issuer shall be eligible to make an initial public offer of specified securities,
 only if:

 (a) the issuer has an operating revenue, based on consolidated audited
 accounts, of at least USD twenty million in the last financial year or
 averaged over the last three financial years; or

 (b) the issuer has a pre-tax profit, based on consolidated audited accounts,
 of at least USD one million in the last financial year or averaged over
 the last three financial years; or

 (c) The issuer has a post issue market capitalization of at least USD twenty
 five million; or

 (d) It qualifies under any other eligibility criteria specified by the
 Authority.

 Explanation: “Financial year” for the purposes of these regulations shall mean
 financial year followed by the issuer in accordance with the applicable laws of
 its home jurisdiction.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 9, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.6
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Before a company can do an IPO (sell its shares to the public for the first time) on an IFSC exchange, it must clear a basic financial test. It only needs to pass one of these three: (1) yearly sales of at least USD 20 million, (2) yearly profit before tax of at least USD 1 million, or (3) a total market value of at least USD 25 million after the IPO. For the first two, it uses its audited group accounts — either the last year, or the three-year average. A young or loss-making company that fails the sales and profit tests can still qualify on market value alone, but it will have to justify that value convincingly, because the merchant banker (lead manager) and the regulator will question it.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The tests are alternatives, not cumulative — one satisfied limb is enough. The market-cap limb (limb c) is the escape route for pre-revenue or loss-making issuers, but it shifts the burden to a defensible post-issue valuation, which the Authority and lead manager will probe. 'Financial year' follows the issuer's home-jurisdiction convention, so a non-March year-end is acceptable if applied consistently.
regulation_content.practical_point: Test all three limbs on audited consolidated numbers before committing to offer costs; where only the market-cap limb works, prepare the valuation basis and comparable analysis to support it.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Keep audited consolidated accounts and the eligibility computation for each limb on file for lead-manager and Authority review.
regulation_content.example: A software start-up has only USD 6 million in sales and is making losses. It fails tests (1) and (2). It can still do its IPO under test (3) if its value after listing believably reaches USD 25 million — provided that valuation survives hard questioning.
regulation_content.risk_point: The weak spot is a thin or over-optimistic valuation used to pass the market-value test. Expect the merchant banker and regulator to probe how that number was arrived at.
regulation_content.interview_point: A loss-making company with USD 5 million sales wants to IPO. Which of the three tests can it use, and what will it need to prove?
regulation_content.important_numbers: Operating revenue ≥ USD 20 million; pre-tax profit ≥ USD 1 million; post-issue market cap ≥ USD 25 million; measured on last FY or 3-FY average
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers making an initial public offer of specified securities in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
10. SR Equity Shares

 An issuer, which has issued SR equity shares, shall be allowed to make an initial
 public offer of its ordinary shares for listing on a recognised stock exchange,
 subject to the conditions that:

 (a) The issue of SR equity shares had been authorised by a resolution
 passed at a general meeting of the shareholders of the issuer; and

 (b) The SR equity shares have been held for a period of at least three
 months prior to the filing of the draft offer document.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 10, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.7
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Some companies have special shares that carry extra voting power ('SR' shares). A company like this can still do a normal IPO, but only if two things are true: the shareholders formally approved these special shares in a meeting, and the shares were held for at least 3 months before the IPO paperwork was filed. Both conditions exist to show the special-voting setup was genuine and not created at the last minute just to keep control after listing.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The conditions are guardrails against last-minute control engineering ahead of listing. The three-month holding and prior general-meeting authorisation together evidence that the differential-rights structure pre-dates the listing decision rather than being manufactured for it.
regulation_content.practical_point: Verify the general-meeting authorisation and the three-month holding clock against the intended DRHP filing date before locking the offer timetable.
regulation_content.important_numbers: SR equity shares held ≥ 3 months before filing draft offer document
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers making an initial public offer of specified securities in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
11. Offer for Sale

 (1) In case of an offer for sale, the specified securities must have been held by
 the existing holders for a period of at least one year prior to the date of filing
 of the draft offer document:

 Provided that in case equity shares received on conversion are being
 offered for sale, the holding period of convertible securities or depository
 receipts, as the case may be, and the holding period of resultant equity
 shares, together, shall be considered for the purpose of calculation of the
 period of one year.

 Explanation: Where equity shares arising out of conversion are being offered
 for sale, such conversion should be completed prior to filing of the offer
 document and full disclosures of the terms of conversion should be made in the
 draft offer document.

 (2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-regulation (1), the requirement
 of holding equity shares for a period of one year shall not apply:

 (a) Where the equity shares offered for sale were acquired pursuant to any
 scheme of merger or amalgamation in lieu of business and invested
 capital which had been in existence for a period of more than one year
 prior to approval of such scheme; or

 (b) Where the equity shares offered for sale were issued under a bonus
 issue on securities held for a period of at least one year prior to the
 filing of the draft offer document with the Authority, and also subject
 to the following:

 (i) such equity shares being issued out of free reserves and share
 premium existing in the books of account as at the end of the
 financial year preceding the financial year in which the draft
 offer document is filed with the Authority; and

 (ii) such equity shares not being issued by utilisation of
 revaluation reserves or unrealized profits of the issuer.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 11, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.7
regulation_content.simple_explanation: An 'offer for sale' is when existing shareholders sell their own shares to the public (rather than the company issuing new ones). To do this, they must have held those shares for at least 1 year before filing the IPO paperwork. Time held before converting other instruments into these shares counts too. The 1-year wait is relaxed for shares received through an approved merger, or as bonus shares on long-held shares (subject to conditions). The point is to stop people who just picked up shares from quickly offloading them onto the public.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The one-year seasoning stops recently-acquired stock being flipped to the public through an OFS. The bonus and merger carve-outs prevent the rule catching genuinely long-held economic interest that merely changed form; the free-reserves and no-revaluation-reserve conditions are what keep the carve-out honest.
regulation_content.practical_point: For each selling shareholder, prepare a simple timeline showing when they got their shares and confirming the 1-year mark is crossed. Track conversions and bonus shares carefully, since they change the start date.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Retain evidence of acquisition dates, conversion terms and the source of any bonus issue (free reserves / share premium) for each OFS seller.
regulation_content.risk_point: Inspection tests whether the seasoning clock was correctly computed across conversions and bonus issues, and whether carve-outs were applied only where the conditions were truly met.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Offer-for-sale holding period ≥ 1 year before filing draft offer document
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers making an initial public offer of specified securities in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
12. Lead manager

 The issuer shall appoint lead manager(s) to the issue and other intermediaries in
 consultation with the lead manager(s).
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 12, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.8
regulation_content.simple_explanation: The company must hire one or more merchant bankers (lead managers) to run the IPO, and pick the other service providers together with them. This appointment matters because almost every later duty — due diligence, filings, post-issue work — runs through the lead manager.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The lead manager is the anchor of the issue's accountability chain — every downstream due-diligence, filing and post-issue obligation runs through this appointment.
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers making an initial public offer of specified securities in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.provision_heading: In-principle approval from recognised stock exchange(s)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
13. In-principle approval from recognised stock exchange(s)

 (1) The issuer shall file an application with a recognised stock exchange
 seeking in-principle approval for listing of specified securities:

 Provided that where the application is made to more than one recognised
 stock exchange, the issuer shall choose one of them as the designated stock
 exchange.

 (2) The recognised stock exchange shall grant an in-principle approval or reject
 the application within fifteen days from the date of receipt of complete
 application from the issuer.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 13, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.8
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Before the IPO, the company must get 'in-principle' (preliminary) approval from a stock exchange. If it approaches more than one exchange, it names one as the main ('designated') exchange. The exchange must say yes or no within 15 days of getting a complete application — so if the application is incomplete, that clock simply does not start. Pick the designated exchange early, because several later duties are tied to it.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The fifteen-day clock runs from a complete application, so an incomplete filing simply resets the wait rather than pressuring the exchange. Choosing the designated exchange early matters because several later obligations attach to it specifically.
regulation_content.practical_point: File a complete in-principle application and diarise the fifteen-day window; designate the exchange before circulating the offer timetable.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Record the in-principle application, the completeness confirmation and the approval/rejection within the fifteen-day window.
regulation_content.important_numbers: In-principle approval / rejection within 15 days of complete application
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers making an initial public offer of specified securities in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
14. Filing of Offer Document

 (1) Where size of the proposed issue is USD fifty million or below,

 (a) the issuer, through the lead manager(s), shall file a draft offer document
 along with applicable fee with the Authority;

 (b) the lead manager(s) shall also submit a due diligence certificate along
 with the draft offer document;

 (c) the draft offer document shall be hosted on the websites of the
 Authority, the recognised stock exchange(s) where the specified
 securities are proposed to be listed, the issuer and the lead manager(s)
 of the issue.

 (2) Where size of the proposed issue is more than USD fifty million,

 (a) the issuer, through the lead manager(s), shall file a draft offer document
 along with applicable fee with the Authority;

 (b) the lead manager(s) shall also submit a due diligence certificate along
 with the draft offer document;

 (c) the draft offer document shall be hosted on the websites of the
 Authority, the recognised stock exchange(s) where the specified
 securities are proposed to be listed, the issuer and the lead manager(s)
 for seven working days, inviting comments from public;

 (d) the lead manager(s) shall file with the Authority details of material
 comments received by them or by the issuer from the public on the
 draft offer document during such period and the consequential
 changes, if any, that are proposed to be made pursuant thereto, in the
 draft offer document;

 (e) the Authority may issue observations, if any, on the draft offer
 document within twenty-one working days from the later of the
 following dates:

 (i) the date of receipt of the draft offer document; or

 (ii) the date of receipt of satisfactory reply from the issuer
 and/or the lead manager(s) where the Authority has sought
 any clarification or additional information from them; or

 (iii) the date of receipt of clarification or information from any
 regulator or agency, where the Authority has sought any
 clarification or information from such regulator or agency;
 or

 (iv) the date of receipt of a copy of in-principle approval given
 by the recognised stock exchange(s).

 (f) the issuer shall carry out changes advised by the Authority, if any, in
 the draft offer document;

 (g) the issuer shall, through the lead manager(s), file the updated offer
 document with the Authority and the recognised stock exchange(s)
 prior to going ahead with the issue.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 14, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.8
regulation_content.simple_explanation: This explains how the IPO disclosure document is filed, and it splits by deal size. If the issue is USD 50 million or smaller: the company files a draft document and fee with the regulator, the lead manager gives a due-diligence certificate, and the document goes on the relevant websites. If the issue is bigger than USD 50 million: on top of that, the document is put up for 7 working days for public comments, the lead manager reports the key comments and any changes, and the regulator may send its comments ('observations') within 21 working days — after which the company files the updated document. Important: filing does not mean the regulator has approved whether the IPO is a good investment.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The USD 50 million line is the real fork in the timetable — above it, you inherit a public-comment window and an observations cycle; at or below it, you do not. The twenty-one-working-day observation clock runs from the latest of four trigger dates, so incomplete replies to the Authority quietly extend the timeline rather than breaching it. Filing is for record; it is not clearance of commercial merit (the Reg 16(5) disclaimer says as much).
regulation_content.practical_point: First fix the issue size against the USD 50 million line, because that decides which track you are on. For larger issues, build the 7-day comment window and the observations cycle into your timetable, and answer every regulator query quickly to keep the 21-day clock clean.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Retain the exact filed version, the due-diligence certificate, the filing acknowledgement, fee proof, public comments received, and every subsequent amendment in the transaction record.
regulation_content.example: An issue of USD 60 million crosses the USD 50 million line. So the draft document must be open for public comments for 7 working days, and the regulator can issue its observations within 21 working days before the company moves ahead.
regulation_content.risk_point: Common findings: treating filing as approval, mis-sizing the issue to dodge the comment window, and losing track of which trigger date started the observation clock.
regulation_content.interview_point: An issue starts at USD 45 million but is later increased to USD 55 million. What extra steps kick in once it crosses USD 50 million?
regulation_content.important_numbers: Issue-size threshold: USD 50 million; public comment period 7 working days (above threshold); Authority observations within 21 working days
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers making an initial public offer of specified securities in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
15. Offer Timing

 The offer shall be made by the issuer within a period of not more than twelve
 months from the date of issuance of observations by the Authority:

 Provided that if the proposed size of the issue is USD fifty million or below, the
 period of twelve months shall be from the date of receipt of offer document by
 the Authority:

 Provided further that if the offer is not made within the specified time period, a
 fresh draft offer document shall be filed with the Authority and the recognised
 stock exchange(s).
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 15, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.9
regulation_content.simple_explanation: An IPO has a shelf life. The company must actually launch the offer within 12 months of the regulator's observations (or, for issues of USD 50 million or below, within 12 months of the regulator receiving the document). Miss that window and there is no extension — you have to prepare and file a fresh draft document.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The start of the twelve-month clock tracks the filing track under Reg 14 — observations for larger issues, receipt for smaller ones. Missing it is not fatal but expensive: you re-file rather than extend.
regulation_content.practical_point: Diarise the twelve-month long-stop from the correct start date and build launch contingencies well inside it.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Offer to be made within 12 months of observations (or of receipt of offer document, for issues ≤ USD 50 million)
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers making an initial public offer of specified securities in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 16, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.9
regulation_content.simple_explanation: This is the big 'what must go in the IPO document' rule. The document must give investors full, correct and useful information — risk factors, who owns the company (listing anyone with 5% or more), details of the issue, financials, deals with related parties, court cases and group companies — backed by the lead manager's due diligence. Key conditions: financials for at least the last 3 years (fewer if the company is younger), and the financial information cannot be older than 180 days when the IPO launches. A standard IFSCA warning line must be printed word-for-word, in bold. Note: that 180-day limit was raised from 135 days on 14 October 2025, giving companies a bit more breathing room.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The 180-day staleness cap was raised from 135 days with effect from 14-Oct-2025, giving issuers a modestly longer runway between audited numbers and launch — plan the audit-to-launch window against 180, not the older figure. The reconciliation-to-IFRS requirement for home-standard financials is the item that most often surfaces late and delays filing. Note the disclaimer is a verbatim, bold, non-negotiable inclusion.
regulation_content.practical_point: Plan the timing so the financial numbers are still within 180 days on launch day. If the company uses its home-country accounting standards, get the conversion to IFRS done early — this is the item that most often causes last-minute delays. And copy the IFSCA warning line exactly, in bold.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Owner: issuer and lead manager(s). Maintain the due-diligence record, the materiality policy, the ≥5% shareholder schedule, and the audited/limited-reviewed financials evidencing the ≤180-day age at launch.
regulation_content.example: A company plans to launch its IPO but its latest audited accounts will be 200 days old on launch day. That breaks the 180-day limit. It must either refresh the numbers (a fresh audit or limited review) or bring the launch date forward.
regulation_content.risk_point: Common problems inspectors find: financials older than 180 days, the warning line missing or reworded, and home-standard accounts filed without the required IFRS conversion.
regulation_content.interview_point: A company's audited accounts will be 190 days old on launch day. What are its options, and how did the October 2025 change help?
regulation_content.important_numbers: Capital-structure disclosure at ≥5% pre-issue holders; audited financials for ≥3 FYs; financial information not older than 180 days (w.e.f. 14-Oct-2025; earlier 135 days)
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers making an initial public offer of specified securities in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
17. Reservations

 The issuer may choose to make reservations out of the issue size in favour of
 the following categories of persons and the same shall suitably be disclosed in
 the offer document:

1 Substituted for the words “one hundred and thirty five” by the IFSCA (Listing)
(Amendment) Regulations, 2025, w.e.f. 14th October, 2025.

 (a) employees;

 (b) directors; and

 (c) shareholders (other than controlling shareholders) of its group entities
 which are listed.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 17, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.11
regulation_content.simple_explanation: The company may set aside a part of the IPO for its own employees and directors, and for shareholders of its listed group companies — but not for controlling shareholders of those group companies. This 'reservation' is optional, and the list of who can get it is fixed, so nobody can quietly reserve shares for themselves. Whatever is reserved must be disclosed in the IPO document.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: Reservations are permissive, not mandatory, and the categories are closed — controlling shareholders of group entities are deliberately excluded to prevent self-allocation dressed as a reservation.
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers making an initial public offer of specified securities in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
18. Pricing

 The issuer shall determine pricing, in consultation with the lead manager(s),
 either through fixed price or book building process and shall suitably disclose
 the same in the offer document:

 Provided that in case of listing of equity shares by a public Indian company, the
 issuer shall also comply with the requirements prescribed under schedule XI of
 the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-debt Instruments) Rules, 2019.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 18, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.12
regulation_content.simple_explanation: The IPO price is decided by the company together with the lead manager, either as a fixed price or through 'book building' (where investor bids help set the price), and the method is disclosed. If it is an Indian public company listing shares, the price must also respect India's FEMA pricing rules.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The FEMA overlay bites again for Indian issuers — pricing freedom under IFSCA is still fenced by the NDI pricing framework for a public Indian company.
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers making an initial public offer of specified securities in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
19. Offer period

 The initial public offer shall be kept open for at least one working day and not
 more than ten working days:

 Provided that in case the issuer has made a simultaneous offer in any other
 jurisdiction, the offer period may be for same period as applicable in the other
 jurisdiction.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 19, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.12
regulation_content.simple_explanation: An IPO must stay open for at least 1 working day and no more than 10 working days. If the same offer is also running in another country at the same time, the company can match that country's window instead, so the two offers stay in step.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The simultaneous-offer flex exists so a dual-track international offering is not forced into two inconsistent windows.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Offer open ≥1 and ≤10 working days
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers making an initial public offer of specified securities in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
20. Minimum public offer

 (1) Where the issuer is a company incorporated in India, including in an IFSC,
 such issuer shall comply with the minimum offer and allotment to public and
 minimum public shareholding norms prescribed under the Securities Contracts
 (Regulation) Rules, 1957.

 (2) Where the issuer is a company incorporated outside India, the minimum
 offer and allotment to public shall be at least ten per cent. of the post issue capital
 and such issuer shall also maintain the minimum public shareholding of ten per
 cent. of the post issue capital on a continuous basis.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 20, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.12
regulation_content.simple_explanation: How much of the company must be offered to the public depends on where it is incorporated. An India-incorporated company (including one in IFSC) follows India's detailed public-shareholding rules (the SCRR). A company incorporated outside India follows a simpler test: offer and allot at least 10% of its post-IPO shares to the public, and keep at least 10% in public hands at all times after listing. Do not mix up the two — a company based in IFSC but incorporated in India uses the Indian rules.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The two regimes are genuinely different: Indian-incorporated issuers inherit the full SCRR public-shareholding architecture, while foreign issuers face a flat 10% test. Reading the wrong regime onto the issuer is a classic error where the issuer is in IFSC but incorporated in India.
regulation_content.practical_point: First confirm where the company is incorporated, then apply the right test. For a foreign company, remember the 10% public holding is an ongoing duty to monitor, not a one-time listing box to tick.
regulation_content.risk_point: Continuous MPS breaches by foreign issuers post-listing are a live monitoring risk, not a one-time filing item.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Foreign issuers: minimum public offer and continuous MPS of 10% of post-issue capital
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers making an initial public offer of specified securities in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
21. Minimum subscription

 An offer shall be considered successful only if the minimum subscription as
 disclosed in the offer document is received:

 Provided that the concept of minimum subscription shall apply only to fresh
 issue of specified securities and not for the Offer for Sale component of the
 public offer.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 21, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.12
regulation_content.simple_explanation: An IPO only 'succeeds' if the company receives the minimum subscription (minimum money) it promised in its document. This minimum applies only to the new shares the company is issuing — not to the 'offer for sale' part where existing holders sell — because an offer for sale raises no new money for the company.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The carve-out for OFS is logical — an OFS raises no new capital for the issuer, so a subscription floor keyed to fund-raising need has nothing to bite on there.
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers making an initial public offer of specified securities in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
22. Anchor Investor

 The issuer may offer a portion of the issue size for subscription by an anchor
 investor, by providing relevant disclosures in the offer document such as details
 of anchor investor, proposed maximum limit of allotment to anchor investor,
 lockup (if any), pricing etc.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 22, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.12
regulation_content.simple_explanation: The company can give a slice of the IPO to an 'anchor investor' — a large investor who commits early to signal confidence and help set the price. If it does, the IPO document must disclose who the anchor is, the most they can get, any freeze on their shares, and the price.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: Anchor allocation is a demand-signalling and price-discovery tool; the disclosure list is the transparency price for that early allocation.
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers making an initial public offer of specified securities in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
23. Underwriting

 A public issue of specified securities may be underwritten by an underwriter
 and in such a case, adequate disclosures regarding underwriting arrangements
 shall be disclosed in the offer document.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 23, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.12
regulation_content.simple_explanation: An IPO can be 'underwritten', meaning someone agrees to buy any shares the public does not, so the company is assured of its money. If used, the underwriting arrangement must be clearly disclosed. Here it is optional — unlike the SPAC rules (Reg 51), where part of the underwriter's fee must be held back until the deal completes.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: Underwriting here is optional; contrast the SPAC regime (Reg 51), where deferral of half the commission into escrow is mandatory.
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers making an initial public offer of specified securities in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
24. Monitoring Agency

 (1) The issuer may choose to appoint a credit rating agency registered with the
 Authority or a globally recognised credit rating agency which is registered
 with a regulator in India or a regulator in a Foreign Jurisdiction, as a
 monitoring agency for monitoring the use of proceeds of the issue.

 (2) Where a monitoring agency has been appointed, the issuer shall, within
 forty five days from the end of each quarter, publicly disseminate the report
 of the monitoring agency by uploading the same on its website as well as
 submitting the same to the recognised stock exchange(s) on which its
 specified securities are listed.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 24, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.13
regulation_content.simple_explanation: The company can appoint a credit rating agency as a 'monitoring agency' to keep an eye on how the IPO money is actually spent. Appointing one is optional — but once appointed, the company must publish that agency's report within 45 days after the end of every quarter, on its website and to the exchange. So the choice is only at the start; after that, it becomes a fixed quarterly duty.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: Appointment is optional, but once you appoint, the forty-five-day quarterly disclosure becomes a hard, recurring obligation — the discretion is at the front end only.
regulation_content.practical_point: If you appoint a monitoring agency, set a standing quarterly reminder for the 45-day report and route it through compliance. If you do not appoint one, double-check you never promised investors that you would.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Owner: issuer. Where a monitoring agency is in place, publish its report within 45 days of each quarter-end until the mandate ends.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Monitoring-agency report within 45 days of each quarter-end
regulation_content.compliance_frequency: Quarterly (report within 45 days of quarter-end, where a monitoring agency is appointed)
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers making an initial public offer of specified securities in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
25. Allotment

 (1) Allotment to investors shall be on proportionate basis or discretionary basis
 as decided by the issuer in consultation with the lead manager(s) and
 disclosed in the offer document.

 (2) The issuer and lead manager(s) shall ensure that the specified securities are
 allotted and the payments and refunds are completed within [eight]2
 working days from the date of closing of the issue.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 25, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.13
regulation_content.simple_explanation: After the IPO closes, the company and lead manager must finish allotting shares and completing all payments and refunds within 8 working days. This window was made longer — from 5 to 8 working days — on 14 October 2025, which eases the rush. But 8 working days is a hard deadline, not a target, and delays in refunds or allotment are the kind of thing investors notice and inspectors flag.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The window was widened from five to eight working days with effect from 14-Oct-2025 — a practitioner-friendly change that eases the settlement crunch, but the obligation is still a hard outer limit, not a target.
regulation_content.practical_point: Plan the allotment-and-refund process to finish inside 8 working days, and stop using the old 5-day assumption in your timetables.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Owner: issuer and lead manager(s). Evidence allotment, payment and refund completion within 8 working days of closing.
regulation_content.risk_point: Refund/allotment delays beyond the window are a visible investor-facing breach and a standard inspection checkpoint.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Allotment, payments and refunds within 8 working days of issue closing (w.e.f. 14-Oct-2025; earlier 5)
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers making an initial public offer of specified securities in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
26. Listing

 The issuer shall list its specified securities on the recognised stock exchange(s)
 within such period, as specified by the recognised stock exchange(s):

 Provided that in case the issuer has made a simultaneous offer in any other
 jurisdiction, the specified securities shall be listed on the same date.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 26, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.13
regulation_content.simple_explanation: The company must get listed within the time the exchange sets. If the same offer is also running abroad, listing must happen on the same day in both places, so no market gets an information or trading head start.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: Same-date listing for dual offerings prevents arbitrage and information asymmetry between the two markets.
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers making an initial public offer of specified securities in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
27. Post-issue report

 The issuer, through the lead manager(s), shall file a post-issue report with the
 recognised stock exchange(s) giving details including relating to number, value
 and percentage of all applications received, allotments made, basis of allotment,
 subscription, details of credit of specified securities, details relating to payments
 and refunds, and the date of filing of listing application, within ten working days
 from the date of closing of the issue.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 27, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.13
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Within 10 working days of the IPO closing, the company (through the lead manager) files a 'post-issue report' with the exchange. This report ties up the loose ends — how many applied, how shares were allotted, subscription levels, when shares were credited, and payments and refunds. It is the final reconciliation confirming what was promised actually happened.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The post-issue report is the reconciliation that closes the loop on the offer — it is where subscription and allotment representations meet the settlement reality.
regulation_content.practical_point: Assign the post-issue report to the lead manager with a ten-working-day deadline and reconcile it against the allotment and refund records under Reg 25.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Owner: issuer (through lead manager). File the post-issue report within 10 working days of closing.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Post-issue report within 10 working days of issue closing
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers making an initial public offer of specified securities in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.provision_heading: Price stabilisation through green shoe option
regulation_content.regulation_text:
28. Price stabilisation through green shoe option

 (1) An issuer may provide a green shoe option for stabilising the post listing
 price of its specified securities, subject to the following conditions:

 (a) the draft offer document contains all material disclosures about the
 green shoe option;

2 Substituted for the word “five” by the IFSCA (Listing) (Amendment) Regulations, 2025,

w.e.f. 14th October, 2025.

 (b) the issuer has appointed an investment banker or a broker dealer
 registered with the Authority as a stabilising agent, who shall be
 responsible for the price stabilisation process;

 (c) the maximum number of specified securities that may be borrowed
 from pre-issue shareholders for the purpose of allotment or allocation
 of specified securities shall not exceed 15% of the total issue size.

 (2) The price stabilisation process shall be available for a period not exceeding
 ninety days from the date of obtaining trading permission from the
 recognised stock exchange(s) in respect of the specified securities allotted
 in the public issue.

 (3) The stabilising agent shall open a special account, distinct from the issue
 account, with a Banking Unit for crediting the monies received from the
 applicants against the over-allotment and a special account with a
 depository participant for crediting specified securities to be bought from
 the market during the stabilisation period out of the monies credited in the
 special bank account.

 (4) The specified securities bought from the market shall be returned to the pre-
 issue shareholders promptly and not later than two working days after the
 end of the stabilization period.

 (5) On expiry of the stabilisation period, if the stabilising agent has not been
 able to buy specified securities from the market to the extent of such
 securities over-allotted, the issuer shall allot specified securities at issue
 price to the extent of the shortfall within five working days of the closure
 of the stabilisation period and such specified securities shall be returned to
 the pre-issue shareholders by the stabilising agent in lieu of the specified
 securities borrowed from them and the demat account with the depository
 participant shall be closed thereafter.

 (6) The issuer shall make a listing application in respect of the further specified
 securities allotted under sub-regulation (5), to all the recognised stock
 exchanges where the specified securities allotted in the public issue are
 listed.

 (7) Any monies left in the special bank account after remittance of monies to
 the issuer and deduction of expenses incurred by the stabilising agent for
 the stabilisation process shall be transferred to the pre-issue shareholders
 who lent their specified securities towards the green shoe option, and the
 special bank account shall be closed soon thereafter.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 28, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.13
regulation_content.simple_explanation: A 'green shoe' is a tool to steady the share price just after listing. The company can allot a few extra shares (borrowed from big pre-IPO shareholders) and later buy shares in the market to support the price. There are firm limits: the extra shares cannot exceed 15% of the issue; price-support activity can run for up to 90 days; borrowed shares must be returned within 2 working days after that period; any shortfall is made up by issuing fresh shares at the IPO price within 5 working days; and special bank and demat accounts are opened and closed for the purpose. A registered 'stabilising agent' runs the whole thing.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The mechanism is a tightly-plumbed escrow-and-return cycle, not a licence to trade. The three hard numbers — 15% cap, 90-day window, and the return/shortfall settlement clocks — are what an inspection reconstructs; the stabilising agent's account discipline is where control failures show up.
regulation_content.practical_point: If you use a green shoe, appoint the stabilising agent early, put the share-borrowing agreement with big shareholders in writing, and set up the special accounts and the return process in advance around the 90-day and 2/5-day deadlines.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Owner: stabilising agent / issuer. Maintain the borrowing agreement, special bank and demat account records, and evidence of returns/shortfall allotment within the prescribed windows.
regulation_content.example: On a USD 40 million IPO, the company can over-allot up to USD 6 million of shares (15%), support the price for up to 90 days, and must then return the borrowed shares within 2 working days — issuing fresh shares at the IPO price within 5 working days to cover any gap.
regulation_content.risk_point: Inspectors focus on the 15% cap, the money trail through the special accounts, and whether borrowed shares were returned to the lending shareholders on time.
regulation_content.interview_point: If the stabilising agent cannot buy back all the extra shares within the 90-day window, how is the gap filled?
regulation_content.important_numbers: Over-allotment ≤15% of issue size; stabilisation ≤90 days; securities returned ≤2 working days after stabilisation; shortfall allotment within 5 working days
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers making an initial public offer of specified securities in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
29. Lockup of securities

 (1) The pre-issue shareholding of promoters and controlling shareholders of the
 issuer shall be locked-up for a period of one hundred and eighty days from
 the date of allotment in the initial public offer:

 Provided that the lockup provisions shall not apply with respect to the
 specified securities lent to stabilising agent for the purpose of green shoe
 option, during the period starting from the date of lending of such specified
 securities and ending on the date on which they are returned to the lender.

 (2) The shareholding of the SR Equity Shares shall be locked-up after the initial

 public offering, until the later of:

 a) their conversion to ordinary shares; and

 b) One year from the date of allotment in the initial public offer.

 (3) The specified securities that are locked-up may be pledged as a collateral
 security:

 Provided that such lockup shall continue pursuant to the invocation of the
 pledge and the transferee shall not be eligible to transfer the specified
 securities till the lockup period stipulated in these regulations has expired.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 29, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.14
regulation_content.simple_explanation: After the IPO, the shares held by promoters and controlling shareholders are frozen ('locked up') and cannot be sold for 180 days. Special extra-voting (SR) shares are frozen for longer — until they convert into ordinary shares or 1 year passes, whichever is later. These shares can be pledged as loan security, but the freeze still applies: even if the lender takes the shares, they cannot sell them until the lock-up ends.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: Two distinct clocks operate — 180 days for ordinary promoter/controlling stock and a longer, conversion-linked clock for SR shares — reflecting the greater control concern around differential-rights capital. The pledge carve-out is narrow: you can encumber, but you cannot use the pledge to defeat the lock-up.
regulation_content.practical_point: In the depository system, tag each frozen block with the right clock — 180 days for ordinary promoter shares, the longer clock for SR shares — and flag any pledge so the freeze survives if the lender calls it in.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Owner: promoters and controlling shareholders. Maintain lock-up records by clock and ensure depository lock markers align with allotment dates.
regulation_content.risk_point: The mistakes inspectors catch are putting SR shares on the shorter 180-day clock, or a pledge arranged to release shares early.
regulation_content.interview_point: A promoter holds both ordinary and SR shares. How long is each frozen, and can either be pledged during the freeze?
regulation_content.important_numbers: Promoter/controlling-shareholder lock-up 180 days from allotment; SR equity shares locked-up till conversion or 1 year, whichever later
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers making an initial public offer of specified securities in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
30. Other responsibilities of lead manager

 (1) The lead manager(s) shall prepare a schedule, listing the activity-wise
 allocation of responsibilities relating to the issue, the name of the lead
 manager(s) responsible for each set of activities or sub-activities, and
 disclose the same in the offer document.

 (2) A lead manager shall be designated for coordinating with the Authority and
 shall be responsible for ensuring that all intermediaries fulfil their
 obligations and functions as specified in their agreements with the issuer.

 (3) The responsibilities of the lead manager(s) shall continue for all pre and
 post-issue activities related to the issue.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 30, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.15
regulation_content.simple_explanation: The lead manager must set out, in writing, who is responsible for which part of the IPO, and — when there are several lead managers — one is named to be the single point of contact with the regulator. The lead manager stays responsible for both the run-up to the IPO and the work after it. Get that responsibility chart and the named coordinator agreed before filing.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: Where there are multiple lead managers, the designated coordinator is the single accountable point for the Authority — get that designation and the responsibility grid on paper before filing, not after.
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers making an initial public offer of specified securities in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
31. Prohibition on payment of incentives

 Any person connected with the issue shall not offer or receive any incentive,
 whether direct or indirect, in any manner, whether in cash or kind or services or
 otherwise to or from any person for making an application in the public offer,
 except for fees or commission for services rendered in relation to the issue.

PART B: FOLLOW-ON PUBLIC OFFER
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 31, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.15
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Nobody involved in the IPO may offer or take any inducement — cash, gifts, free services, anything — to get someone to apply for shares. The only thing allowed is a genuine fee for real work done. The rule targets payments meant to buy demand, so a 'marketing' or 'advisory' payment that suspiciously tracks who applied is exactly what gets scrutinised.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The prohibition targets inducement of demand, not payment for genuine services; the line between a service fee and a disguised incentive is exactly where enforcement attention sits.
regulation_content.risk_point: Structured 'marketing' or 'advisory' payments that correlate with subscription are the classic disguised-incentive risk.
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers making an initial public offer of specified securities in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
32. Applicability
