 A Listed Entity may make a follow-on public offer of specified securities in the
 manner provided in these regulations.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 32, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.15
regulation_content.simple_explanation: This confirms that an already-listed company can raise more money from the public through a 'follow-on public offer' (FPO). It is the doorway into the FPO chapter; the working details are in the next few rules, many of them borrowed from the IPO rules.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: This is the gateway to Part B; the substantive FPO machinery sits in Regs 33 to 39, much of it applied mutatis mutandis from the IPO chapter.
regulation_content.applicability: Listed Entities making a follow-on public offer

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
33. Offer for sale

(1) In case of an offer for sale, the specified securities must have been held by the
 existing holders for a period of at least one year prior to the date of filing of the
 draft offer document:

 Provided that in case equity shares received on conversion are being offered for
 sale, the holding period of convertible securities or depository receipts, as the
 case may be, and the holding period of resultant equity shares together shall be
 considered for the purpose of calculation of the period of one year.

 Explanation: Where equity shares arising out of conversion are being offered
 for sale, such conversion should be completed prior to filing of the offer
 document and full disclosures of the terms of conversion should be made in the
 draft offer document.

(2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-regulation (1), the requirement of
 holding equity shares for a period of one year shall not apply:

 a) Where the equity shares offered for sale were acquired pursuant to any
 scheme of merger or amalgamation in lieu of business and invested
 capital which had been in existence for a period of more than one year
 prior to approval of such scheme; or

 b) Where the equity shares offered for sale were issued under a bonus
 issue on securities held for a period of at least one year prior to the
 filing of the draft offer document with the Authority, and also subject
 to the following:

 (i) such equity shares being issued out of free reserves and share
 premium existing in the books of account as at the end of the
 financial year preceding the financial year in which the draft
 offer document is filed with the Authority; and

 (ii) such equity shares not being issued by utilisation of
 revaluation reserves or unrealized profits of the issuer.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 33, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.15
regulation_content.simple_explanation: The same 1-year holding rule that applies to an IPO's 'offer for sale' also applies to an FPO — existing shareholders must have held their shares for at least a year before the paperwork is filed, with the same treatment for converted, merged and bonus shares. Read this together with the IPO version (Reg 11).
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The FPO OFS rule mirrors the IPO rule almost word for word; read the two together so the seasoning logic is applied consistently across both routes.
regulation_content.applicability: Listed Entities making a follow-on public offer

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
34. Lead manager

 The issuer shall appoint lead manager(s) to the issue and other intermediaries in
 consultation with the lead manager(s).
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 34, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.16
regulation_content.simple_explanation: For an FPO, the company again hires one or more lead managers and picks the other service providers with them — the same setup as an IPO (Reg 12). The lead manager carries the same due-diligence and filing responsibility.
regulation_content.applicability: Listed Entities making a follow-on public offer

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.provision_heading: In-principle approval from recognised stock exchange(s)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
35. In-principle approval from recognised stock exchange(s)

 (1) The issuer shall file an application with a recognised stock exchange
 seeking in-principle approval for listing of specified securities:

 Provided that where the application is made to more than one recognised
 stock exchange, the issuer shall choose one of them as the designated stock
 exchange.

 (2) The recognised stock exchange shall grant an in-principle approval or reject
 the application within fifteen days from the date of receipt of complete
 application from the issuer.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 35, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.16
regulation_content.simple_explanation: An FPO also needs preliminary ('in-principle') approval from a stock exchange, with the same rule about naming a main exchange if more than one is approached, and the same 15-day decision window as an IPO.
regulation_content.applicability: Listed Entities making a follow-on public offer

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
36. Fast track follow-on public offer

 (1) An issuer may make follow-on public offer through the fast track route, if
 the issuer satisfies the following conditions:

 (a) equity shares of the issuer have been listed on a recognised stock
 exchange for a period of at least eighteen months;

 (b) issuer has complied with all the regulatory requirements
 specified by the Authority and the recognised stock exchange(s)
 in the preceding three years;

 (c) no show-cause notice has been issued and pending against the
 issuer or its promoters or controlling shareholders or whole-time
 directors by the Authority or any other financial sector regulator;

 (d) there is no adverse opinion, disclaimer of opinion, qualified
 opinion by the auditors on the financial statements of the issuer,
 or any of the issuer's subsidiaries or associates (having a material

 impact on the issuer's consolidated accounts), in the preceding
 three years;

 (e) there has not been any disclosure relating to irregularities having
 a material impact on the issuer, by any director, key managerial
 personnel or compliance officer.

 Explanation: Where the issuer is listed for a period of less than three
 years, the period under clause (b) and (d) shall be calculated from the
 date of initial listing.

 (2) The issuer, through the lead manager(s), shall file the offer document along
 with applicable fee with the Authority.

 (3) The lead manager(s) shall also submit a due diligence certificate along with
 the offer document.

 (4) The issuer shall simultaneously file the offer document with the recognised
 stock exchange(s).

 (5) The offer document shall be hosted on the websites of the Authority, the
 recognised stock exchange(s), the issuer and the lead manager(s) of the
 issue.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 36, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.16
regulation_content.simple_explanation: A 'fast-track' FPO is a quicker route, but only for companies with a clean record. To use it, the company must clear all five gates: shares listed for at least 18 months; full compliance over the last 3 years; no pending show-cause notice against the company or its top people; no bad or qualified audit report in the last 3 years; and no reported irregularity that had a material impact. It then files the document (with fee and a due-diligence certificate), files with the exchange at the same time, and puts the document up. If the company has been listed for under 3 years, the 3-year look-backs run from its first listing date.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: Fast-track substitutes a clean compliance and audit track record for the fuller observation cycle — the trade is speed for a higher eligibility bar. Where the issuer has been listed under three years, the three-year look-backs run from initial listing, which is the nuance most candidates miss.
regulation_content.practical_point: Run the five fast-track gates as a checklist well before launch. Watch for a stale reading of 'no pending show-cause notice' or a qualified audit report in the look-back window — either one knocks the company off the fast-track route.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Owner: issuer / lead manager. Evidence each fast-track condition (listing tenure, compliance record, no SCN, clean audit opinions, no material irregularity) at filing.
regulation_content.example: A company listed for 20 months with a spotless record qualifies on the listing-tenure gate. But because it has been listed under 3 years, its compliance and audit look-backs are measured from its first listing date, not just the last 3 calendar years.
regulation_content.risk_point: A stale or optimistic reading of 'no pending show-cause notice' or a qualified audit opinion in the look-back window will collapse fast-track eligibility.
regulation_content.interview_point: A company listed for 22 months had a qualified audit report two years ago. Can it use the fast-track FPO, and from when is the look-back counted?
regulation_content.important_numbers: Fast-track FPO: shares listed ≥18 months; compliance track record over preceding 3 years
regulation_content.applicability: Listed Entities making a follow-on public offer

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.provision_heading: Follow-on public offer without fast track
regulation_content.regulation_text:
37. Follow-on public offer without fast track

 The issuer not meeting the conditions for a fast track follow-on public offer,
 may make follow-on public offer by filing the draft offer document in the same
 manner as applicable for Initial Public Offers under PART A of this Chapter.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 37, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.17
regulation_content.simple_explanation: If a company fails any of the fast-track gates, it does its FPO the long way — filing the draft document just like a first-time IPO, with the full comment-and-observations cycle.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: This is the default FPO path — fail any fast-track gate and you fall back into the full IPO-style filing and observation cycle.
regulation_content.applicability: Listed Entities making a follow-on public offer

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.provision_heading: Disclosures in the offer document for a follow-on public offer
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 38, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.17
regulation_content.simple_explanation: This lists what an FPO document must contain — much like the IPO list (risk factors, ownership from 5% up, financials, and so on), plus the lead manager's due diligence and the same bold IFSCA warning line. A helpful shortcut: an already-listed company can point to its recent prospectus or recent exchange filings instead of repeating everything, as long as that information is still current and complete.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The reference-incorporation Explanation is the practical time-saver: an already-listed issuer can cross-refer recent disclosures rather than rebuild them, provided currency and completeness are preserved.
regulation_content.practical_point: Use the shortcut of referring to recent filings where you can, but first confirm they are up to date and complete, and reproduce the warning line word-for-word in bold.
regulation_content.applicability: Listed Entities making a follow-on public offer

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: PUBLIC OFFER OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES (IPO AND FPO)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
39. Issue Process

 The provisions relating to offer timing, pricing, offer period, minimum
 subscription, anchor investor, underwriting, monitoring agency, allotment,
 listing, post-issue report, other responsibilities of lead manager and prohibition
 on payment of incentives provided for Initial Public Offers under PART A of
 this Chapter shall mutatis mutandis apply to follow-on public offer under this
 Chapter.

 CHAPTER IV: LISTING OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES WITHOUT
 PUBLIC OFFER
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 39, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.18
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Rather than repeat them, this rule simply says a big block of the IPO rules also applies to FPOs — timing, pricing, offer period, minimum subscription, anchor investor, underwriting, monitoring agency, allotment, listing, post-issue report, lead-manager duties and the no-inducement rule. So read the FPO chapter with those IPO rules open beside it.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: A single mutatis mutandis hook carries a large block of IPO machinery into the FPO — read Part B always with the referenced IPO provisions open beside it.
regulation_content.applicability: Listed Entities making a follow-on public offer

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: LISTING OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES WITHOUT PUBLIC OFFER
regulation_content.provision_heading: Listing of specified securities without public offer
regulation_content.regulation_text:
40. Listing of specified securities without public offer

 An issuer may list its specified securities on a recognised stock exchange
 without making public offer in the manner as may be specified by the Authority.

CHAPTER V: LISTING OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES ALREADY LISTED
 IN OTHER JURISDICTION
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 40, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.19
regulation_content.simple_explanation: A company can list its shares without doing a public offer at all, in the way the regulator specifies. This is just an enabling door — the actual conditions live in separate regulator instructions, so treat it as a pointer to those.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: An enabling shell — the operative conditions live in whatever the Authority specifies, so treat this as a pointer to separate circulars rather than a self-contained route.
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers listing specified securities without a public offer

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: LISTING OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES ALREADY LISTED IN OTHER JURISDICTION
regulation_content.regulation_text:
41. Secondary Listing without public offer

 An issuer, having its specified securities listed in a jurisdiction outside IFSC,
 may list those specified securities on a recognised stock exchange(s), without
 making public offer, subject to the following conditions:

 (a) It shall file listing application, in the manner specified by the
 recognised stock exchange(s); and

 (b) It shall comply with the listing requirements of the recognised stock
 exchange(s) and such other conditions as may be specified by the
 Authority.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 41, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.19
regulation_content.simple_explanation: A company whose shares are already listed in another country can get a 'secondary listing' in IFSC without a fresh public offer — by filing a listing application and meeting the exchange's requirements plus any regulator conditions. Because it leans on the home listing, the company must keep complying with its home market too; the IFSC requirements sit on top.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: Secondary listing leans on the home listing — the IFSC exchange's requirements sit on top of continued home-market compliance rather than replacing it.
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers with specified securities already listed in a jurisdiction outside IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: LISTING OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES ALREADY LISTED IN OTHER JURISDICTION
regulation_content.regulation_text:
42. Listing with public offer

 (1) An issuer, having its specified securities listed in a jurisdiction outside
 IFSC, may list the specified securities on a recognised stock exchange(s)
 through a public offer.

 (2) The provisions relating to appointment of lead manager, in-principle
 approval from recognised stock exchanges, filing of offer document, offer
 timing, disclosures in offer document, reservations, pricing, offer period,
 minimum public offer, minimum subscription, anchor investor,
 underwriting, monitoring agency, allotment, listing, post-issue report, price
 stabilisation through green shoe option, lockup of securities, other
 responsibilities of lead manager and prohibition on payment of incentives
 provided for Initial Public Offers under PART A of Chapter III shall
 mutatis mutandis apply to listing by way of public offer:

 Explanation: For the purpose of initial disclosures, the issuer may submit
 the disclosures in draft offer document by providing references to a recent
 prospectus or other disclosures made with any stock exchange or any
 regulatory body.

 (3) A public Indian company, with dual listing in IFSC and in India, shall

 comply with the additional regulatory requirements as may be specified by
 the Authority.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 42, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.19
regulation_content.simple_explanation: A company already listed abroad can instead come to IFSC through a public offer, using the IPO rules (with the shortcut of referring to recent disclosures). If it is an Indian public company holding both an IFSC and an Indian listing, it must also meet any extra requirements the regulator sets — the IFSC listing does not switch those off.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The dual-listing overlay for Indian public companies is the item to watch — an IFSC listing does not switch off the additional Indian requirements the Authority may specify.
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers with specified securities already listed in a jurisdiction outside IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: LISTING OF SPECIFIED SECURITIES ALREADY LISTED IN OTHER JURISDICTION
regulation_content.regulation_text:
43. Qualified Institutions Placements

 A public Indian company having its equity shares listed on a stock exchange in
 India may be permitted to make a qualified institutions placement in the manner
 as may be specified by the Authority from time to time.

 CHAPTER VI: LISTING OF SPECIAL PURPOSE ACQUISITION
 COMPANIES (SPAC)
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 43, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.20
regulation_content.simple_explanation: An Indian public company whose shares are listed on an Indian exchange can raise money from big institutional investors through a 'qualified institutions placement' (QIP), in the manner the regulator specifies. The detailed mechanics are left to the regulator, so this is a doorway pending those instructions.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: Another enabling pointer — the QIP mechanics are left to Authority specification, so there is no self-standing process to run here yet.
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers with specified securities already listed in a jurisdiction outside IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: LISTING OF SPECIAL PURPOSE ACQUISITION COMPANIES (SPAC)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
44. Eligibility

 (1) A SPAC is eligible to raise capital through initial public offer of specified
 securities on the recognised stock exchange(s), only where:

 (a) the target business combination has not been identified prior to the
 IPO;

 (b) The SPAC has the provisions for redemption and liquidation in line
 with these Regulations; and

 (c) The sponsor of the SPAC has a good track record in SPAC
 transactions, business combinations, fund management or investment
 banking activities and the same shall be disclosed in the offer
 document.

 Explanation: For the purpose of this chapter, sponsor shall mean a person
 sponsoring the formation of the SPAC and shall include persons holding
 any specified securities of the SPAC prior to the IPO.

 (2) A SPAC shall not be eligible to list specified securities under these
 regulations if the issuer or any of its sponsors is:

 (a) debarred from accessing the capital market; or

 (b) a wilful defaulter; or

 (c) a fugitive economic offender.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 44, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.20
regulation_content.simple_explanation: A SPAC is a 'blank-cheque' company: it raises money from the public first and finds a business to buy later. To do a SPAC IPO, three things must be true — no target business has been picked before the IPO; the SPAC has proper rules for giving money back (redemption) and for winding up (liquidation); and the sponsor (the person setting up and backing the SPAC) has a solid track record, disclosed in the document. Because there is no business yet, investors are really betting on the sponsor, so the sponsor's record and clean status carry the weight. The SPAC is barred if it or its sponsors are banned from markets, wilful defaulters or fugitive offenders.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The 'no target identified' condition is the definitional heart of a SPAC — a blank-cheque vehicle. Sponsor track record substitutes for an operating history, so the diligence weight shifts onto the sponsor's record and fit-and-proper status.
regulation_content.practical_point: Get written proof that no target has been identified or discussed before the IPO, and document the sponsor's track record and clean background up front.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Owner: issuer / sponsors. Maintain the declaration of no pre-IPO target, sponsor track-record evidence, and clean-status confirmations.
regulation_content.example: A sponsor sets up a SPAC to raise USD 100 million and go hunting for a tech company to merge with. It must be able to show it has not already lined up a target — because a pre-arranged deal, even an informal one, breaks the core condition.
regulation_content.risk_point: A pre-existing understanding with a target, however informal, is the fatal integrity risk for a SPAC IPO.
regulation_content.interview_point: Why is 'no target picked before the IPO' the defining condition for a SPAC, and how would you prove it?
regulation_content.important_numbers: SPAC eligibility conditions (no target identified pre-IPO; redemption/liquidation provisions; sponsor track record)
regulation_content.applicability: Special Purpose Acquisition Companies and their sponsors

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: LISTING OF SPECIAL PURPOSE ACQUISITION COMPANIES (SPAC)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
45. IPO Process

 The provisions relating to appointment of lead manager, in-principle approval
 from recognised stock exchange(s) and filing of offer document provided for
 Initial Public Offers under PART A of Chapter III shall mutatis mutandis apply
 to initial public offer by a SPAC.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 45, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.20
regulation_content.simple_explanation: The IPO steps for appointing the lead manager, getting preliminary approval and filing the document apply to a SPAC IPO in the same way (borrowed from Regs 12-14).
regulation_content.applicability: Special Purpose Acquisition Companies and their sponsors

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: LISTING OF SPECIAL PURPOSE ACQUISITION COMPANIES (SPAC)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
46. Offer Timing

 The offer shall be made by the issuer within a period of not more than twelve
 months from the date of issuance of observations by the Authority:

 Provided that if the offer is not made within the specified time period, a fresh
 draft offer document shall be filed.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 46, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.20
regulation_content.simple_explanation: A SPAC must launch its offer within 12 months of the regulator's observations, or file a fresh document — the same shelf-life rule as a normal IPO.
regulation_content.applicability: Special Purpose Acquisition Companies and their sponsors

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: LISTING OF SPECIAL PURPOSE ACQUISITION COMPANIES (SPAC)
regulation_content.provision_heading: Initial disclosures in the Offer Document
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 47, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.20
regulation_content.simple_explanation: A SPAC's IPO document must give investors full and correct material information, plus a set of SPAC-specific details: their right to get money back, what happens on winding up, the sponsor's record, the type of business or region the SPAC will hunt in (without naming an actual target), how long it has to complete a deal, and how it will value a target. Investors are told how the vehicle will behave precisely because nobody can yet tell them what it will buy.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The disclosure architecture is built around the blank-cheque risk — investors are told how the vehicle will behave (redemption, liquidation, timeline, valuation approach) precisely because they cannot be told what it will buy.
regulation_content.practical_point: Structure the SPAC offer document around the redemption/liquidation/timeline disclosures and ensure no target is named while still disclosing the sector or geography focus.
regulation_content.applicability: Special Purpose Acquisition Companies and their sponsors

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: LISTING OF SPECIAL PURPOSE ACQUISITION COMPANIES (SPAC)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
48. Issue size

 (1) The issue shall be of size not less than USD fifty million or any other
 amount as may be specified by the Authority from time to time.

 (2) The sponsors shall hold at least fifteen per cent. (15%) and not more than
 twenty per cent. (20%) of the post issue paid up capital;

 (3) Prior to an IPO, the sponsor shall have aggregate subscription (all
 securities) in the SPAC amounting to USD ten million or an amount
 equivalent to at least two and half per cent. (2.5%) of the issue size,
 whichever is lower; or any other threshold as may be specified by the
 Authority.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 48, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.22
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Three numbers set the size of a SPAC and the sponsor's own stake. The SPAC must raise at least USD 50 million. The sponsor must hold between 15% and 20% of the shares after the IPO. And before the IPO, the sponsor must put in either USD 10 million or 2.5% of the issue size — whichever is lower. That 'whichever is lower' means the sponsor's minimum cheque does not balloon as the SPAC gets bigger.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: Three numbers define sponsor skin-in-the-game and scale: the USD 50 million floor, the 15%–20% sponsor band, and the USD 10 million / 2.5%-whichever-lower pre-IPO commitment. The 'whichever lower' cuts the sponsor's minimum cheque as the issue grows, keeping the commitment proportionate rather than punitive on large SPACs.
regulation_content.practical_point: Work out the sponsor's numbers against all three tests early — the 15%-20% band and the 'lower of USD 10 million / 2.5%' investment drive the share structure and the escrow size. Watch that the sponsor's holding does not drift outside 15%-20% after the IPO.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Owner: issuer / sponsors. Retain the issue-size and sponsor-holding computations and reconcile them to the final offer document.
regulation_content.example: For a USD 200 million SPAC, the sponsor's pre-IPO investment is the lower of USD 10 million or 2.5% (which is USD 5 million) — so USD 5 million. And the sponsor must hold 15%-20% of the post-IPO shares.
regulation_content.risk_point: Sponsor holding drifting outside the 15%–20% band post-issue, or under-committing pre-IPO, are the numeric breaches to watch.
regulation_content.interview_point: For a USD 400 million SPAC, what is the least the sponsor must invest before the IPO, and why does 'whichever is lower' matter as the SPAC grows?
regulation_content.important_numbers: Minimum issue size USD 50 million; sponsors hold 15%–20% of post-issue paid-up capital; pre-IPO sponsor subscription USD 10 million or 2.5% of issue size, whichever lower
regulation_content.applicability: Special Purpose Acquisition Companies and their sponsors

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: LISTING OF SPECIAL PURPOSE ACQUISITION COMPANIES (SPAC)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
49. Pricing

 The issue shall be through a fixed price mechanism and the issuer shall
 determine the price in consultation with the lead manager(s).
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 49, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.22
regulation_content.simple_explanation: A SPAC's shares are sold at a fixed price, set by the company with the lead manager. Book building is not allowed here — a blank-cheque company has no business results yet, so there is nothing for the market to price-discover; a fixed price is the honest option.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: Book-building is deliberately excluded — a blank-cheque vehicle has no operating fundamentals to price-discover, so fixed price is the honest mechanism.
regulation_content.applicability: Special Purpose Acquisition Companies and their sponsors

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: LISTING OF SPECIAL PURPOSE ACQUISITION COMPANIES (SPAC)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
50. Offer period

 The initial public offer shall be kept open for at least one working day and not
 more than ten working days.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 50, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.22
regulation_content.simple_explanation: A SPAC's IPO must stay open for at least 1 and no more than 10 working days — the same window as a normal IPO.
regulation_content.applicability: Special Purpose Acquisition Companies and their sponsors

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: LISTING OF SPECIAL PURPOSE ACQUISITION COMPANIES (SPAC)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
51. Underwriting

 (1) A public issue of specified securities may be underwritten by an underwriter
 and in such a case adequate disclosure regarding underwriting
 arrangements shall be made in the offer document.

 (2) At least fifty per cent. (50%) of the underwriting commission shall be
 deferred until successful completion of the business combination, and shall
 be deposited in the escrow account.

 (3) In case of liquidation, the underwriter shall have no right on the deferred
 commission deposited in the escrow account.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 51, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.22
regulation_content.simple_explanation: A SPAC IPO can be underwritten, but at least half the underwriter's fee must be parked (in escrow) and paid only when the SPAC actually completes its business deal. If the SPAC winds up without a deal, the underwriter loses that held-back fee. This ties the underwriter's reward to getting a deal done — stronger than an ordinary IPO, where underwriting is optional and fully paid.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: Mandatory deferral aligns the underwriter with deal completion rather than mere fund-raising — unlike the optional, fully-payable underwriting in an ordinary IPO (Reg 23). The forfeiture-on-liquidation rule sharpens that alignment.
regulation_content.practical_point: Write the underwriting agreement so at least half the fee sits in escrow, is released only when the deal completes, and is forfeited on winding up. A fee that is mostly paid upfront defeats the purpose.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Owner: issuer. Evidence the deferred-commission escrow arrangement and its completion-contingent release terms.
regulation_content.risk_point: An underwriting fee structure that front-loads more than half the commission defeats the alignment the provision requires.
regulation_content.applicability: Special Purpose Acquisition Companies and their sponsors

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: LISTING OF SPECIAL PURPOSE ACQUISITION COMPANIES (SPAC)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
52. Application and Allotment

 (1) The minimum application size in an initial public offer of SPAC shall be
 USD one hundred thousand.

 (2) Allotment to investors shall be on proportionate basis or discretionary basis,
 as disclosed in the offer document.

 (3) The issuer and lead manager(s) shall ensure that the specified securities are
 allotted, and the payments and refunds are completed within [eight]3
 working days from the date of closing of the issue.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 52, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.23
regulation_content.simple_explanation: In a SPAC IPO, each investor must apply for at least USD 100,000 — this keeps the offer to serious, sophisticated investors, which suits the higher risk of a blank-cheque company. Shares can be allotted proportionally or at the SPAC's discretion (as disclosed), and allotment, payments and refunds must finish within 8 working days of closing (raised from 5 on 14 October 2025).
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The USD 100,000 minimum ticket keeps the SPAC IPO in institutional/HNI territory, matching the sophistication a blank-cheque risk demands. The allotment window moved from five to eight working days with effect from 14-Oct-2025, mirroring the IPO change.
regulation_content.practical_point: Enforce the USD 100,000 minimum at the application stage and settle everything within 8 working days, keeping the allotment record in line with the escrow position.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Owner: issuer and lead manager(s). Evidence the minimum-ticket enforcement and settlement within 8 working days of closing.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Minimum application USD 100,000; allotment/refunds within 8 working days of closing (w.e.f. 14-Oct-2025; earlier 5)
regulation_content.applicability: Special Purpose Acquisition Companies and their sponsors

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: LISTING OF SPECIAL PURPOSE ACQUISITION COMPANIES (SPAC)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
53. Other provisions

 The provisions relating to listing, post-issue report, other responsibilities of lead
 manager and prohibition on payment of incentives provided for Initial Public
 Offers under PART A of Chapter III shall mutatis mutandis apply to initial
 public offer under this Chapter.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 53, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.23
regulation_content.simple_explanation: The IPO rules on listing, the post-issue report, lead-manager duties and the no-inducement rule also apply to a SPAC IPO (borrowed from Regs 26, 27, 30 and 31).
regulation_content.applicability: Special Purpose Acquisition Companies and their sponsors

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: LISTING OF SPECIAL PURPOSE ACQUISITION COMPANIES (SPAC)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
54. SPAC specific obligations

 (1) The SPAC shall ensure that the entire proceeds of the IPO are kept in an
 interest-bearing escrow account controlled by an independent custodian
 until consummation of the SPAC’s business combination.

 (2) The proceeds kept in the escrow account shall be invested only in short-
 term investment grade liquid instruments, as disclosed in the offer
 document.

 (3) The interest and other income derived from the proceeds placed in the
 escrow account may be withdrawn by the SPAC only for the following
 purposes:

 (a) Payment of taxes; and

 (b) General working capital expenses subject to prior approval by way of
 special resolution of the shareholders other than sponsors.

 (4) The SPAC shall seek shareholders’ approval on the proposed business
 combination and shall file a detailed prospectus with the recognised stock
 exchange(s) containing all relevant disclosures including the following:

 (a) Information about the target company(ies) shall include overview of
 industry and business, organisational structure, board of directors,
 management and key managerial personnel (KMPs), major
 shareholders, material shareholders’ agreements, audited financial
 statements for at least previous three financial years, outstanding
 material litigations against the company and its directors and KMPs,
 potential conflicts of interest and other material information;

3 Substituted for the word “five” by the IFSCA (Listing) (Amendment) Regulations, 2025,

w.e.f. 14th October, 2025.

 (b) Information about the business combination transaction including
 valuation of the entities and the methodologies used for valuation;

 (c) Information about the process involved in the business combination
 and the various regulatory and statutory approvals required for
 completion of the transaction;

 (d) Information about the resultant company that would be formed after
 completion of the business combination; and

 (e) Any other information as may be required by the recognised stock
 exchange(s) or the Authority.

(5) The SPAC shall seek prior approval from majority of shareholders other
 than sponsors, for the proposed business combination.

(6) A shareholder (other than sponsors) who has voted against the proposed
 business combination, shall have the redemption right for converting his
 securities into a pro rata portion of the aggregate amount held in the escrow
 account (net of taxes payable).

 Explanation: A SPAC may have the option to not afford the redemption
 right to the shareholders who have not voted.

(7) In the event of change in control of the SPAC, it shall provide the
 redemption option to the shareholders (other than sponsors) for converting
 their securities into a pro rata portion of the aggregate amount held in the
 escrow account (net of taxes payable).

(8) The SPAC shall complete the business combination within the timeline
 disclosed in the offer document, which shall not exceed thirty six months
 from the date of listing on the recognised stock exchange(s).

(9) Where the business combination is not completed within the specified time
 frame, the escrow account shall be liquidated, and specified securities shall
 be delisted in the manner as disclosed in the offer document:

 Provided that, in the event of liquidation and delisting, the sponsors shall
 not participate in the liquidation distribution.

(10) A sponsor shall not transfer or sell any of his specified securities prior to
 the completion of a business combination.

(11) The SPAC shall ensure that the businesses combination has an aggregate
 fair market value of at least eighty per cent. (80%) of the amount deposited
 in the escrow account, excluding deferred underwriting commissions held
 in escrow plus any taxes payable on the income earned on the escrowed
 funds.

(12) The SPAC and the sponsors shall ensure that there is no related party
 transaction or connection of sponsor or any of their associates with the
 business combination.

(13) Where warrants have been issued in the IPO, the SPAC shall comply with
 the following:

 (a) Each unit shall consist of one share and not more than one share
 purchase warrants;

 (b) The exercise price of the warrants shall not be lower than the price of
 the equity shares offered in the IPO;

 (c) The warrants and the equity shares may be traded separately on the
 recognised stock exchanges, as per the details disclosed in the offer
 document;

 (d) The warrants shall not be exercisable prior to the completion of the
 business combination;

 (e) In case of liquidation of SPAC, the warrants shall expire; and

 (f) The warrants shall not have any entitlement to the funds lying in the
 escrow account upon liquidation or redemption.

 (14) The Authority may, from time to time, specify additional requirements
 regarding listing of SPACs on the recognised stock exchange(s).
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 54, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.23
regulation_content.simple_explanation: This is the SPAC rulebook that protects investors' money until a deal happens. All the IPO money goes into a protected account (escrow) run by an independent custodian, invested only in safe, short-term instruments. Interest can be taken out only for taxes and — with special approval from the non-sponsor investors — for running costs. To buy a business, the SPAC needs shareholder approval, a detailed document, and the backing of a majority of non-sponsor investors. Investors who disagree can take their money back, and so can everyone if control changes. The deal must be completed within the promised time, capped at 36 months from listing; if it is not, the SPAC winds up and delists — and the sponsors get nothing from the wind-up. The target business must be worth at least 80% of the escrow money, cannot be a related party, and there are strict limits on warrants (a bonus right to buy shares later). In short: independent-custodian escrow, a non-sponsor vote, and the right to exit are the core protections; the 36-month deadline and 80% value test are the core numbers.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: This is the operational spine of the SPAC. The load-bearing numbers are the 36-month completion long-stop and the 80% FMV floor; the load-bearing controls are the independent-custodian escrow, the non-sponsor voting gate, and the dissenter redemption right. Sponsors are structurally subordinated on the downside — excluded from liquidation distribution and barred from pre-completion transfers — which is the accountability design candidates should be able to explain.
regulation_content.practical_point: Set up the escrow, the independent custodian and the safe-investment rules first. Then build the process for the non-sponsor vote and the exit (redemption) right. Track the 36-month clock from listing and test any target against the 80% value rule and the not-a-related-party rule before signing.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Owner: SPAC / sponsors. Maintain escrow and custodian records, permitted-investment evidence, shareholder-approval documentation, redemption records, and the FMV computation against escrow.
regulation_content.example: A SPAC holds USD 150 million in escrow. Any business it buys must be worth at least USD 120 million (80% of the escrow), the deal must close within 36 months of listing, and any investor who votes no can take back their share of the escrow money.
regulation_content.risk_point: Inspectors focus on whether the escrow was truly protected, whether the 80% value test was met, whether the 36-month clock was respected, and whether the exit right worked as promised.
regulation_content.interview_point: Walk through what happens to the escrow money, the sponsors and the public investors if a SPAC fails to complete a deal within 36 months.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Business combination FMV ≥80% of escrow; completion ≤36 months from listing; warrants: 1 share + ≤1 warrant per unit
regulation_content.applicability: Special Purpose Acquisition Companies and their sponsors

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: LISTING OF SPECIAL PURPOSE ACQUISITION COMPANIES (SPAC)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
55. Continuous disclosure requirements

 The continuous disclosure requirements applicable for Listed Entities as
 specified under Chapter XII of these regulations shall mutatis mutandis apply to
 a SPAC.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 55, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.25
regulation_content.simple_explanation: From the day it lists, a SPAC must follow the ongoing disclosure duties in Chapter XII, just like any other listed company. Being a blank-cheque company does not let it delay those duties.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: A SPAC is a Listed Entity for continuous-disclosure purposes from listing — the blank-cheque status does not defer LODR obligations.
regulation_content.applicability: Special Purpose Acquisition Companies and their sponsors

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: LISTING OF SPECIAL PURPOSE ACQUISITION COMPANIES (SPAC)
regulation_content.regulation_text:
56. Post business combination

 (1) The resultant entity shall immediately disclose details regarding the
 completed transaction to the recognised stock exchange(s).

 Explanation: For the purpose of this chapter, the resultant entity means the
 issuer resulting from the completion of the business combination by the
 SPAC.

 (2) The resultant entity shall be required to meet the listing eligibility criteria
 set out in these regulations within one hundred and eighty days, in order to
 continue listing on the recognised stock exchange(s).

 (3) The resultant entity shall comply with the listing obligations and continuous
 disclosure requirements specified under Chapter XII of these regulations.

 (4) The shareholding of the sponsors of the SPAC in the resultant entity shall
 be locked up for a period of one year from the date of closing of the business
 combination.

 (5) The shareholding of the controlling shareholders, directors and key
 managerial personnel of the resultant entity shall be locked up for a period
 of one year from the date of closing of the business combination.

 CHAPTER VII: RIGHTS ISSUE, PREFERENTIAL ISSUE AND
 QUALIFIED INSTITUTIONS PLACEMENT
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 56, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.25
regulation_content.simple_explanation: After the SPAC completes its business deal, it must disclose the deal at once. The merged ('resultant') company then has 180 days to meet the normal listing eligibility tests if it wants to stay listed — this stops a SPAC being used as a back door to list a company that could not qualify on its own. The merged company must follow Chapter XII, and the sponsor plus the merged company's controlling shareholders, directors and top managers are frozen from selling for 1 year from the deal's close.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The 180-day eligibility test is the gate that stops a SPAC being used to back-door a non-qualifying company onto the exchange — the resultant entity must independently clear listing eligibility. The one-year lock-ups on sponsors and control persons align them with the post-deal entity.
regulation_content.practical_point: From the deal's closing date, diarise the 180-day deadline and confirm the merged company genuinely meets listing eligibility. Apply the 1-year sale freeze to the sponsor and the control group.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Owner: resultant entity. Evidence eligibility compliance within 180 days and lock-up records for sponsors, controlling shareholders, directors and KMP.
regulation_content.risk_point: A resultant entity that cannot meet listing eligibility within 180 days faces continuation risk — this is the post-deal cliff to monitor.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Resultant entity to meet listing eligibility within 180 days; sponsor and controlling/KMP lock-up 1 year from closing of business combination
regulation_content.applicability: Special Purpose Acquisition Companies and their sponsors

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: RIGHTS ISSUE, PREFERENTIAL ISSUE AND QUALIFIED INSTITUTIONS PLACEMENT
regulation_content.provision_heading: Rights Issue, Preferential Issue and Qualified Institutions Placement
regulation_content.regulation_text:
57. Rights Issue, Preferential Issue and Qualified Institutions Placement

 A Listed Entity may make rights issues, preferential issues or qualified
 institutions placement of specified securities, subject to compliance with the
 requirements that may be specified by the Authority.

 CHAPTER VIII: LISTING OF DEPOSITORY RECEIPTS
PART A: ELIGIBILITY
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 57, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.25
regulation_content.simple_explanation: A listed company can raise more money through a rights issue, a preferential issue or a QIP, subject to the requirements the regulator specifies. The detailed steps are left to the regulator, so this is a doorway pending those instructions.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: An enabling provision — the operative mechanics are left to Authority specification, so treat this as a gateway pending detailed norms.
regulation_content.applicability: Listed Entities making rights / preferential issues or QIP

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.regulation_text:
58. Eligibility

 An issuer incorporated outside an IFSC shall be eligible to make an issue of
 depository receipts only if -

 (i) It is authorised to issue depository receipts as per the
 applicable laws of its home jurisdiction; and

 (ii) The underlying securities represented by such depository
 receipts is in dematerialised form, fully paid and free from all
 encumbrances.

PART B: PUBLIC OFFER OF DEPOSITORY RECEIPTS
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 58, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.26
regulation_content.simple_explanation: A depository receipt (DR) is a certificate traded in one country that represents shares held in another. To issue DRs here, the company must be incorporated outside IFSC and allowed under its home law to issue DRs, and the underlying shares must be in electronic form, fully paid, and free of any charge or pledge. That last point matters: the receipt can only be as clean as the shares behind it.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The encumbrance-free, fully-paid condition on the underlying is the integrity anchor for the DR — the receipt can be no cleaner than the security it represents.
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers of depository receipts

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.regulation_text:
59. Offer size

 The issue of depository receipts shall be of size not less than USD seven hundred
 thousand, or any other amount as may be specified by the Authority.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 59, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.26
regulation_content.simple_explanation: A DR issue must be at least USD 700,000 (or another amount the regulator sets). This is a deliberately low floor, so smaller issues can use the DR route.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The USD 700,000 floor is deliberately modest, opening the DR route to smaller issuances than the equity IPO thresholds contemplate.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Depository receipts issue size ≥ USD 700,000
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers of depository receipts

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.regulation_text:
60. Filing of Draft Offer Document

 The filing of draft offer document shall be in the manner as specified for filing
 of offer document for initial public offer under PART A of Chapter III of these
 Regulations.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 60, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.26
regulation_content.simple_explanation: The draft DR document is filed the same way as an IPO document (following Reg 14's filing steps).
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers of depository receipts

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.provision_heading: Initial disclosures in the Offer Document
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 61, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.26
regulation_content.simple_explanation: A DR document must give investors the usual full information, plus DR-specific details — about the underlying shares and, crucially, what rights DR holders actually have (how dividends and voting reach them through the depository). It also needs 3 years of audited accounts (fewer if the company is younger), with the latest set no more than 12 months old. The DR-holder-rights part is where investors most often misunderstand, so it deserves care.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The DR disclosure adds a layer the equity IPO does not — the rights of DR holders versus the underlying, including dividend and voting mechanics through the depository, which is where investor misunderstanding concentrates. Note the DR financial-currency test is twelve months, not the 180-day cap that applies to specified-securities IPOs.
regulation_content.practical_point: Pay special attention to explaining DR-holder rights and how the depository works, and check the latest accounts are within 12 months (note: this is 12 months, not the 180-day limit used for ordinary share IPOs).
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers of depository receipts

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.regulation_text:
62. Pricing

 The issuer may determine price of the depository receipts in consultation with
 the lead manager(s) through fixed price or book building process.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 62, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.28
regulation_content.simple_explanation: DRs are priced by the company with the lead manager, either at a fixed price or through book building — the same choice as an ordinary IPO.
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers of depository receipts

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.regulation_text:
63. Offer period

 The initial public offer of depository receipts shall be kept open for at least one
 working day and not more than ten working days.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 63, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.28
regulation_content.simple_explanation: A DR offer must stay open for at least 1 and no more than 10 working days — the same window as a share IPO.
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers of depository receipts

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.regulation_text:
64. Minimum subscription

 The listing of depository receipts shall be permitted only if the subscription in
 the offer is not less than USD seven hundred thousand or any other amount as
 may be specified by the Authority.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 64, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.28
regulation_content.simple_explanation: DRs can be listed only if the offer actually brings in at least USD 700,000 (or another amount the regulator sets). This matches the minimum issue size in Reg 59, so the deal must reach the scale it was built for.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The subscription floor mirrors the issue-size floor in Reg 59 — the deal must actually reach the minimum scale it was structured for.
regulation_content.important_numbers: DR listing subscription ≥ USD 700,000
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers of depository receipts

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.regulation_text:
65. Allotment

 The issuer and lead manager(s) shall ensure that the depository receipts are
 allotted, and the payments and refunds are completed within [eight]4 working
 days from the date of closure of the issue.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 65, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.28
regulation_content.simple_explanation: DR allotment, payments and refunds must be completed within 8 working days of the offer closing — raised from 5 on 14 October 2025, in line with the IPO and SPAC changes.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: Widened from five to eight working days with effect from 14-Oct-2025, consistent with the IPO and SPAC allotment changes.
regulation_content.practical_point: Finish DR allotment and refunds within 8 working days, and drop the old 5-day assumption from the plan.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Owner: issuer and lead manager(s). Evidence DR allotment and settlement within 8 working days of closure.
regulation_content.important_numbers: DR allotment/refunds within 8 working days of closure (w.e.f. 14-Oct-2025; earlier 5)
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers of depository receipts

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.regulation_text:
66. Listing

4 Substituted for the word “five” by the IFSCA (Listing) (Amendment) Regulations, 2025,
w.e.f. 14th October, 2025.

 The issuer shall list the depository receipts on the recognised stock exchange(s)
 within such period, as may be specified by the concerned recognised stock
 exchange.

PART C: SECONDARY LISTING WITHOUT PUBLIC OFFER
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 66, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.28
regulation_content.simple_explanation: The company must list the DRs within the time the exchange sets — the DR version of the IPO listing-timing rule.
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers of depository receipts

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.regulation_text:
67. Secondary Listing without Public Offer

 An issuer, having its depository receipts listed in a jurisdiction outside IFSC,
 may list its depository receipts on a recognised stock exchange by filing the
 listing application in such form and manner as may be specified by the
 recognised stock exchange(s).

 CHAPTER IX: LISTING OF DEBT SECURITIES
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 67, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.29
regulation_content.simple_explanation: A company whose DRs are already listed abroad can get a secondary DR listing in IFSC just by filing a listing application in the exchange's format — a lighter route that leans on the existing home listing.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The DR secondary-listing route parallels the specified-securities route in Reg 41 — a lighter, application-led path resting on the home listing.
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers of depository receipts

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.regulation_text:
68. Listing of Debt Securities

 An issuer may list its debt securities on a recognised stock exchange:

 Explanation: The debt securities proposed to be issued and listed on a
 recognised stock exchange may be offered on a standalone basis or through a
 series of issuances (including medium term note programme).
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 68, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.29
regulation_content.simple_explanation: A company can list bonds and other debt on the exchange, either as a single issue or as a series — including under a 'medium-term note programme', a standing setup that lets it issue debt in batches over time without re-doing all the paperwork each time. That programme flexibility is the practical headline here.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The MTN-programme flexibility is the practical headline — it lets an issuer establish a programme and draw down in tranches rather than documenting each issuance from scratch.
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers of debt securities

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.regulation_text:
69. Filing of documents

 (1) The issuer desirous of listing its debt securities on a recognised stock
 exchange shall file the listing application along with a copy of the offer
 document or information memorandum, as applicable, with the recognised
 stock exchange in accordance with the requirements specified by the
 recognised stock exchange.

 (2) The issuer shall file the listing application with a recognised stock exchange
 along with applicable regulatory fee and the same shall be remitted to the
 Authority in the manner specified by the Authority.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 69, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.29
regulation_content.simple_explanation: The company files the listing application with its offer document or information memorandum with the exchange, following the exchange's requirements, and pays the fee, which goes to the regulator. For debt, the exchange leads at the front end, with the regulator in the loop on fees and oversight.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: Debt listing is exchange-led at the front end — the exchange sets the application requirements, with the Authority in the fee and oversight loop.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Owner: issuer. File the listing application, offer document/IM and fee per exchange requirements.
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers of debt securities

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 70, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.29
regulation_content.simple_explanation: This lists what a debt document must disclose, in two buckets: about the company (its business, management, owners, audited accounts, court cases and any past defaults) and about the specific issue (the security details, risks, where it will list, the maximum amount for a programme, and what the money will be used for). Because debt is about getting repaid, the focus is on defaults, any collateral, and use of proceeds. The exchange can waive some disclosures under a written internal policy.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The disclosure set is calibrated to credit risk rather than equity upside — defaults, security/collateral and use of proceeds carry the weight. The exchange's power to exempt certain disclosures, subject to an internal policy, introduces a documented-discretion element worth flagging in diligence.
regulation_content.practical_point: Map the disclosures to the exchange's template, be sure to cover any collateral, and if the exchange waives something, get that waiver documented against its policy rather than assumed.
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers of debt securities

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.provision_heading: Minimum subscription in case of private placement
regulation_content.regulation_text:
71. Minimum subscription in case of private placement

 The minimum subscription amount for an investor in case of private placement
 shall be disclosed in the offer document.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 71, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.30
regulation_content.simple_explanation: For a privately placed debt issue (sold to select investors, not the public), the document must state the minimum amount each investor has to put in. There is no fixed statutory figure — the company sets and discloses it, and the market prices around it.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The floor is disclosure-driven rather than a fixed statutory figure — the issuer sets and discloses it, and the market prices around it.
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers of debt securities

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.regulation_text:
72. Credit Rating

 (1) The issuer shall obtain credit rating for its debt securities proposed to be

 listed on a recognised stock exchange from a credit rating agency registered
 either with the Authority or with a regulator in a Foreign Jurisdiction.

 Provided that from April 01, 2025 or such other date as may be specified
 by the Authority, the issuer shall obtain a credit rating from at least one
 credit rating agency registered with the Authority and may obtain any
 additional credit rating(s) from a globally recognised rating agency which
 is registered with a regulator in a Foreign Jurisdiction.

 (2) The issuer shall disclose details of the ratings, assigned to the debt
 securities, in the prospectus, shelf prospectus or information memorandum,
 as the case may be.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 72, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.30
regulation_content.simple_explanation: The company must get its debt credit-rated (an independent grade of how safely it can repay). From 1 April 2025, at least one rating must come from an IFSCA-registered agency; any extra rating can come from a recognised foreign agency. All ratings go into the offer document. So the issue date decides the rule: from 1 April 2025, a foreign rating on its own is not enough.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The 01-Apr-2025 trigger reshapes the rating architecture — an IFSCA-registered rating becomes mandatory, and a foreign rating alone no longer suffices. Confirm which rating regime applies to the specific issuance date.
regulation_content.practical_point: For any issue on or after 1 April 2025, use an IFSCA-registered rating agency as your main rating and treat a foreign rating as an add-on. A foreign rating alone, after that date, is a straight breach.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Owner: issuer. Obtain and disclose the required rating(s), ensuring an IFSCA-registered rating on/after 01-Apr-2025.
regulation_content.risk_point: Relying on a foreign rating alone for a post-01-Apr-2025 issuance is a direct non-compliance.
regulation_content.interview_point: For a debt issuance priced in May 2025, what is the minimum credit-rating configuration, and how did 01-Apr-2025 change it?
regulation_content.important_numbers: Dual-rating trigger: from 01-Apr-2025, at least one rating from an IFSCA-registered credit rating agency
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers of debt securities

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.regulation_text:
73. Public Issue

 In respect of a public issue of debt securities on a recognised stock exchange,
 the issuer shall comply with requirements such as appointment of trustee,
 creation of debenture redemption reserve and such other requirements as may
 be specified by the Authority or the recognised stock exchange(s).
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 73, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.31
regulation_content.simple_explanation: For a public debt issue (sold to the general public), the company must also meet extra investor-protection requirements the regulator or exchange sets — such as appointing a trustee (who safeguards bondholders' interests) and creating a redemption reserve. These protections are not automatically required for private placements.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: Public debt issuance imports the classic investor-protection scaffolding — trustee and redemption reserve — that private placements do not necessarily carry.
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers of debt securities

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.regulation_text:
74. Exempt Issuers

 A recognised stock exchange may, if satisfied on the basis of an application
 made by an issuer, relax the applicability of certain requirements of this chapter
 or chapter X, as the case may be, in accordance with its internal policy or
 guidelines, for the following issuers:

 (a) Supranational, multilateral or statutory institutions /organisations
 /agencies;

 (b) Entities whose securities are irrevocably guaranteed by a Sovereign;
 and

 (c) Any other entity as may be specified by the Authority.

CHAPTER X: ENVIRONMENTAL, SOCIAL AND GOVERNANCE (ESG)
 LABELLED DEBT SECURITIES
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 74, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.31
regulation_content.simple_explanation: The exchange can, under a written policy, relax some Chapter IX or X requirements for very high-quality public issuers — like multilateral institutions, government-guaranteed issuers, and others the regulator names. The exchange's internal policy keeps this discretion disciplined.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The relaxation is a proviso mechanism for high-credit-quality public issuers — the exchange's internal policy is the control that keeps the discretion principled.
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers of debt securities

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: ENVIRONMENTAL, SOCIAL AND GOVERNANCE (ESG) LABELLED DEBT SECURITIES
regulation_content.regulation_text:
75. Applicability

 (1) This chapter shall apply to Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG)
 labelled debt securities including “green”, “social”, “sustainability”,
 “sustainability linked” debt securities or any other ESG labelled debt
 securities as may be specified by the Authority, which is listed or proposed
 to be listed on a recognised stock exchange.

 (2) The requirements under this chapter shall be in addition to the requirements
 detailed in Chapter IX.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 75, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024 (IFSCA/GN/2024/006, as amended up to 14-Oct-2025); source PDF p.31
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Chapter X applies to ESG-labelled debt — bonds badged as green, social, sustainability or sustainability-linked — that is or will be listed. Importantly, it applies on top of the normal debt rules in Chapter IX, not instead of them. So an ESG bond carries all the usual debt duties plus the ESG ones; treating the ESG chapter as a substitute is a common mistake.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: Chapter X is additive, not alternative — an ESG-labelled bond carries the full Chapter IX debt obligations plus the ESG layer. Treating the ESG chapter as a substitute is a common structuring error.
regulation_content.applicability: Issuers of ESG-labelled debt securities

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Listing) Regulations, 2024
regulation_content.chapter_title: ENVIRONMENTAL, SOCIAL AND GOVERNANCE (ESG) LABELLED DEBT SECURITIES
regulation_content.regulation_text:
76. Recognised Standards

 (1) The debt securities shall be labelled as “green”, “social” or “sustainability”
 only if the funds raised through the issuance of such debt securities are
 proposed to be utilised for financing or refinancing projects and/or assets
 aligned with any of the following recognised standards:

 (a) International Capital Market Association (ICMA) Principles /
 Guidelines;

 (b) Climate Bonds Standard;

 (c) ASEAN Standards;

 (d) European Union Standards;

 (e) Any framework or methodology specified by a competent authority or
 a financial sector regulator in India; or

 (f) Other international standards as may be permitted by the Authority on
 case-by-case basis.

 (2) The debt securities shall be labelled as “sustainability-linked” if they are
 aligned with any of the recognised standards specified under sub-regulation
 (1) or any other such qualifying criteria as may be specified by the
 Authority.

 (3) The issuer shall appoint an independent external reviewer to ascertain that
 the ESG labelled debt securities are in alignment with any of the recognised
 standards mentioned at sub-regulation (1), in compliance with the
 following conditions:

 (a) The reviewer shall be independent of the issuer, its directors, senior
 management, key managerial personnel and advisers;

 (b) The reviewer shall be remunerated in a way that prevents any conflicts
 of interest; and

 (c) The reviewer shall have sufficient expertise in assessing ESG debt
 securities.

 (4) The independent external reviewer mentioned at sub-regulation (3) may
 take one or more of the following forms recommended by International
 Capital Market Association:

 (a) Second Party Opinion;

 (b) Verification;

 (c) Certification;

 (d) Scoring / Rating.
 Explanation: A credit rating agency or an ESG rating provider registered
 with the Authority or a regulator in India or a Foreign Jurisdiction shall also
 be eligible to act as an external reviewer for the purpose of these regulations
 subject to compliance with conditions mentioned at sub-regulation (3).

 (5) The issuer shall ensure that the details regarding the independent external
 reviewer are adequately disclosed and easily accessible to the investors.
